questions.model_answer: UL97 (viral kinase) mutation confers ganciclovir resistance only: high-dose ganciclovir - can sometimes be used (overcome low-level resistance); foscarnet - yes (active); cidofovir - yes (active). UL54 (viral DNA polymerase) mutation confers cross-resistance to ganciclovir, foscarnet, and cidofovir: high-dose ganciclovir - no; foscarnet - no (though foscarnet activity depends on the specific UL54 codon); cidofovir - no.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answer marks foscarnet as usable for a UL54 mutation; Mandell states UL54 mutations confer resistance to ganciclovir, foscarnet, and cidofovir, so foscarnet activity cannot be assumed and depends on the specific UL54 mutation.

cohort_answer.text: UL97 mutation - HD ganciclovir: yes; Foscarnet: yes; Cidofovir: yes. UL54 mutation - HD ganciclovir: no; Foscarnet: Yes (not 100% resistant); Cidofovir: no

questions.model_answer: 1) Fluconazole over caspofungin (fluconazole achieves high urinary/renal and CSF levels; echinocandins have negligible urinary penetration). 2) Doxycycline over TMP-SMX (doxycycline is not used to treat CDI and carries low risk of inducing CDI). 3) Valganciclovir over valacyclovir (valganciclovir/ganciclovir has potent anti-CMV activity; valacyclovir is poorly active against CMV). 4) Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem (carbapenems interact with anti-epileptics, lowering levels, so the non-carbapenem beta-lactam is preferred). 5) Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin (per exam key, for a CNS bacterial infection; ampicillin over cloxacillin is also defensible for Listeria meningitis). 6) Atovaquone over dapsone (dapsone causes oxidant hemolysis in G6PD deficiency).

cohort_answer.text:
Acyclovir over valacyclovir: HSV meningitis/encephalitis.
Valganciclovir over valacyclovir: Herpes B treatment better activity, CMV treatment.
Famciclovir over acyclovir: Uncomplicated zoster (famciclovir higher oral bioavailability than acyclovir, dosed TID rather than 5 times daily).
Atovaquone over dapsone: G6PD deficiency, Toxoplasmosis.
Doxycycline over TMP-SMX: Someone on Ramipril and Spironolactone with MRSA infection may want Doxycycline over TMP/SMX given risk of hyperkalemia.
Fluconazole over caspofungin: Cryptococcus not covered by echinocandins, urinary or CNS infections.
Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate: CNS infections, disseminated histoplasmosis, suspected mucormycosis.
Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem: Enterococcus.
Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin: Anaerobic activity is best with moxi.
Metronidazole over clindamycin: Bacteroides fragilis, increasing clinda resistance.
Azithromycin over clarithromycin: Better for gram-negatives, esp. M catarrhalis and H flu.
Ampicillin over cloxacillin: Enterococci, Listeria.
Cefazolin over cloxacillin: Surgical prophylaxis, penicillin allergy, AIN, heart failure.

questions.model_answer: MOA: Acyclovir is a guanosine nucleoside analogue that is monophosphorylated by the virus-encoded thymidine kinase (TK), then further phosphorylated by cellular kinases to acyclovir triphosphate, which competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and, incorporated into the growing chain, acts as an obligate DNA chain terminator. HSV resistance: most commonly absent/reduced or altered viral TK (cannot phosphorylate the drug), less commonly mutations in viral DNA polymerase. Two alternate drugs: foscarnet and cidofovir (both act independent of viral TK). Non-renal AE: cidofovir - neutropenia (also uveitis/iritis, fever); foscarnet - electrolyte disturbances/seizures.

cohort_answer.text: MOA: Nucleoside analog that inhibits replication of HSV, phosphorylated by virus-encoded TK then inhibits DNA polymerase. Mechanism of Res: Thymidine Kinase - Decrease production or absence of any, Decreased affinity for nucleoside analog. DNA pol - Decreased affinity for nucleoside analog. Two other drugs that can be used: Foscarnet: cytopenia, ha, nausea, seizures, increased liver enz. Cidofovir: nausea, fever, alopecia uveitis/iritis. Nephrotoxicity | HSV-1/2 and VZV; Valacyclovir | Valtrex | Prodrug of ACV | Oral and IV | TTP, nephrotoxicity and HUS | HSV-1/2, VZV and HCMV; Cidofovir | Vistide | DNA chain terminator | IV w/ Probenecid | Renal, neutropenia and fever | HCMV, HSV-1/2 and VZV; Foscarnet | Foscavir | Inhibitor of DNA pol pyrophosphate binding site | IV only | Renal, electrolytes, fever, sz and anemia | HCMV, HSV-1/2 and EBV; Ganciclovir | Cytovene | Guanosine analogue, DNA chain terminator | Oral and IV | Fever, cytopenia (3 lines) and renal | HCMV, HSV-1/2; Valganciclovir | Valcyte | Prodrug of GCV | Oral and IV | Neutropenia, H/A and anemia | HCMV; Letermovir | Prevymis | Inhibitor of terminase complex | Oral and IV | GI, edema and cough | HCMV; Penciclovir | Denavir | Similar to ACV | Topical formulation | H/A and site reaction | HSV-1; Famciclovir | Famvir | Prodrug of PCV | Oral and IV | H/A and GI | HSV-1/2 and VZV; Trifluridine | Viroptic | Not established | Ophthalmic topical | Increased IO pressure and local reaction | HSV-1; Docosanol | Abreva | Prevents HSV entry into cells | Topical formulation | H/A and skin rash | Oral HSV

questions.question: State the mechanism/target of action of the following antivirals: foscarnet, cidofovir, maribavir, and letermovir.
questions.question_raw: PM 10. Mechanism of antivirals. Where do the following act (3): Foscarnet, Cidofovir, Maribavir, Letermovir

parts.text: State the mechanism/target of each antiviral

parts_raw.text: State the mechanism/target of each antiviral

questions.model_answer: Foscarnet: inorganic pyrophosphate analogue that directly inhibits the viral DNA polymerase by binding its pyrophosphate-binding site (no phosphorylation required). Cidofovir: nucleotide analogue activated intracellularly to its diphosphate by cellular (not viral) enzymes; competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and, when incorporated, terminates chain elongation. Maribavir: specific inhibitor of the UL97 protein kinase - blocks phosphorylation of viral proteins (e.g., UL44), inhibiting viral DNA synthesis and nuclear egress of virions. Letermovir: inhibits the CMV terminase enzyme complex (UL51/UL56), blocking cleavage/packaging of unit-length viral DNA; does not require phosphorylation and does not target DNA polymerase.

cohort_answer.text: Foscarnet - DNA polymerase inhibitor; UL54, binds pyrophosphate binding site, inhibits transcription. Cidofovir - intracellularly activated to diphosphate form; competitive DNA polymerase inhibition and incorporated into viral DNA causing chain termination. Maribavir - UL97 phosphokinase inhibitor, inhibits viral DNA synthesis and blocks nuclear egress of virions. Letermovir - UL56, inhibits DNA terminase enzyme complex, stops splicing and virion assembly.

questions.model_answer: Ganciclovir: guanosine analogue phosphorylated first by the CMV UL97 phosphotransferase, then by cellular enzymes, to ganciclovir triphosphate - a competitive inhibitor of dGTP incorporation that preferentially inhibits viral DNA polymerase and slows/stops chain elongation (not an obligate chain terminator). Ganciclovir resistance (2): (1) UL97 mutations/deletions reducing phosphorylation/activation of the drug (most common; usually retains foscarnet and cidofovir susceptibility); (2) UL54 viral DNA polymerase mutations (often with UL97, frequent cross-resistance to cidofovir, usually susceptible to foscarnet). Foscarnet: pyrophosphate analogue that reversibly blocks the pyrophosphate-binding site of viral DNA polymerase, inhibiting replication without requiring phosphorylation. Acyclovir: nucleoside analogue activated by viral TK then cellular kinases to acyclovir triphosphate, which inhibits/inactivates viral DNA polymerase and causes obligate DNA chain termination. Letermovir: inhibits the CMV terminase complex (UL51/UL56), blocking cleavage of concatemeric DNA into unit genomes for packaging; CMV-only, no effect on DNA polymerase.

cohort_answer.text: Ganciclovir: competes with deoxyguanosine triphosphate to inhibit viral DNA polymerase and block viral DNA synthesis; primarily reserved for CMV, also active against HSV-1/2 (same mechanism as valganciclovir). Resistance: UL97 gene mutation (most common, occurs prior to UL54, causes deficiency in viral kinase for ganciclovir phosphorylation/activation, cidofovir and foscarnet usually retain efficacy) and UL54 mutation (often co-exists with UL97, changes viral DNA polymerase, cross-resistance to cidofovir common, cross-resistance to foscarnet rare; HSV isolates resistant to acyclovir due to absent TK are also resistant to ganciclovir). Foscarnet: inorganic pyrophosphate analog, selectively inhibits viral DNA polymerase by blocking pyrophosphate binding sites, suppressing viral replication; resistance occurs secondary to some but not all UL54 mutations; primarily reserved for ganciclovir-resistant CMV, also effective against HSV/VZV including acyclovir-resistant isolates; main adverse effect is nephrotoxicity (dose-limiting, minimized with hydration). Acyclovir: synthetic purine nucleoside analog with high affinity for HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV thymidine kinase which phosphorylates/activates the drug; human cellular guanylate kinase further phosphorylates it to acyclovir triphosphate, which blocks viral DNA synthesis by competitively inhibiting/inactivating viral DNA polymerase and causing DNA chain termination (valacyclovir, penciclovir, famciclovir have similar mechanisms; cidofovir similar but does not require viral TK). Letermovir: inhibits the CMV terminase complex (novel mechanism), which normally cleaves long DNA chains produced during CMV replication into single functional units; only active against CMV; FDA approved for CMV prophylaxis in adult CMV-seropositive allogeneic HSCT recipients; low barrier to resistance in vitro; no dosage adjustment needed with CrCl >10 mL/min.

questions.model_answer: Ganciclovir: activated by the CMV UL97 kinase then cellular kinases to ganciclovir triphosphate, which competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and halts DNA chain elongation. Foscarnet: pyrophosphate analogue that directly blocks the pyrophosphate-binding site of viral DNA polymerase (no phosphorylation needed). Letermovir: inhibits the CMV terminase complex (UL51/UL56), blocking cleavage/packaging of viral DNA. Two ganciclovir-resistance mutations: (1) UL97 - phosphotransferase gene; impairs intracellular phosphorylation/activation of ganciclovir (affects the drug-activation step in the cell; foscarnet/cidofovir usually still active); (2) UL54 - viral DNA polymerase gene; alters the enzyme acting at viral DNA synthesis in the nucleus (frequent cidofovir cross-resistance, foscarnet usually retained).

questions.model_answer: Row 1 - UL97 (phosphotransferase; most common, low-level resistance): High-dose ganciclovir - possible for low-level resistance (reduced efficacy); Foscarnet - YES (active); Cidofovir - YES (active). Row 2 - UL54 (DNA polymerase; often with UL97, high-level resistance): High-dose ganciclovir - NO; Foscarnet - usually YES (active, though some UL54 mutations confer foscarnet resistance); Cidofovir - usually NO (frequent cross-resistance with UL54). Summary: UL97 alone retains foscarnet and cidofovir; combined UL97+UL54 is cross-resistant to cidofovir but usually foscarnet-susceptible.

questions.model_answer: MOA: i) Herpesviridae - pyrophosphate analogue that reversibly blocks the pyrophosphate-binding site of the viral DNA polymerase, inhibiting replication without requiring intracellular phosphorylation. ii) HIV - inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase (a DNA polymerase) at its pyrophosphate-binding site. 4 viruses (other than HIV): CMV (including ganciclovir-resistant strains), HSV (including acyclovir-resistant strains), VZV (including acyclovir-resistant), and EBV (HHV-6 also acceptable). 4 metabolic derangements: hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia, and hypo- or hyperphosphatemia (electrolyte wasting/chelation).
questions.beyond_mandell: Foscarnet's action on HIV reverse transcriptase and the specific electrolyte derangements are standard antiviral pharmacology (Mandell/package insert); the detailed foscarnet toxicity paragraph was outside the provided text slice.

questions.model_answer:
a) Foscarnet is an inorganic pyrophosphate analogue. It binds directly to the pyrophosphate-binding site of the viral DNA polymerase and non-competitively blocks cleavage of pyrophosphate from incoming nucleoside triphosphates, halting viral DNA chain elongation. It needs no activation/phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase, so it retains activity against TK-deficient (acyclovir-resistant) herpesviruses.
b) In HIV it directly inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase at the pyrophosphate-binding site (it is not a nucleoside analogue and is not an NNRTI).
c) (1) Cytomegalovirus (retinitis, ganciclovir-resistant disease) (2) Acyclovir-resistant/TK-deficient HSV (3) Acyclovir-resistant VZV (4) HHV-6 (also active against EBV and HHV-8).
d) (1) Nephrotoxicity (azotemia/acute tubular necrosis) (2) Electrolyte disturbance (hypo- or hypercalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia from divalent-cation chelation) (3) Genital/penile ulceration (4) CNS effects including seizures (also nausea, anaemia).
questions.beyond_mandell: The provided Mandell slice omits the dedicated Foscarnet section (mechanism/toxicity fall in a cut gap); MOA, spectrum and toxicity are from the Mandell ch.46 Foscarnet text / established knowledge. The text does confirm foscarnet inhibits viral DNA polymerase and is used for acyclovir-resistant VZV/HSV and ganciclovir-resistant CMV.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort calls the HIV mechanism an NNRTI; foscarnet inhibits reverse transcriptase at the pyrophosphate-binding site and is not a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor.

cohort_answer.text:
MOA Herpesviridae: Inhibits viral DNA polymerase by binding to the pyrophosphate binding site (non-competitive inhibition).
MOA HIV: Inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase (acts as an NNRTI).
4 other viruses: CMV - retinitis/encephalitis; HSV resistant to acyclovir; VZV - progressive outer retinal necrosis; Human Herpesvirus 6. (Has activity against all Herpesviridae viruses: HSV, VZV, EBV, CMV, HHV-6, HHV-7, Kaposi; not used for HIV in practice; mainly used for CMV, HSV, VZV resistant disease with TK/UL97 resistance.)
4 side effects: Nephrotoxicity (avoid with other nephrotoxic drugs; azotemia, proteinuria, acute tubular necrosis; give with saline prehydration 1-2L NS 1-2h before dosing); electrolyte abnormalities (chelator of divalent cations - hypocalcemia 15-35%, hypomagnesemia 15-44%, hypokalemia 10-16%; also hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, hyperphosphatemia; monitor electrolytes closely); CNS (seizures 10%, headaches 25%); GI (nausea 47%, diarrhea 30%, vomiting 26%); hematological (anemia 33%, granulocytopenia 17%); fever (65%).

questions.model_answer:
a) Acyclovir is a guanosine analogue. It is monophosphorylated selectively by the viral thymidine kinase (TK), then converted by cellular kinases to acyclovir triphosphate, which competitively inhibits the viral DNA polymerase as a dGTP analogue; because acyclovir lacks a 3'-hydroxyl it causes obligate viral DNA chain termination once incorporated.
b) (1) Mutation in the viral thymidine kinase (absent or altered TK) preventing phosphorylation/activation of the drug - the commonest mechanism. (2) Mutation in the viral DNA polymerase.
c) (1) Foscarnet - toxicities: nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbance (hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia), genital ulceration. (2) Cidofovir - toxicities: dose-related nephrotoxicity (proximal tubular dysfunction, proteinuria, azotaemia, occasionally Fanconi syndrome) and neutropenia (~24%).
questions.beyond_mandell: Acyclovir phosphorylation/chain-termination detail and foscarnet toxicities are established knowledge; the text (p.579) gives the TK and DNA-polymerase resistance mechanisms and that acyclovir is an obligate chain terminator, and (p.584) the cidofovir toxicity profile.

cohort_answer.text: a) Binds DNA polymerase to stop DNA synthesis: acyclovir phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase, then cellular kinase to acyclovir-triphosphate, which competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase as dGTP analog; incorporation causes chain termination. b) Mutation in DNA polymerase (target); mutation in viral kinase (prevents activation, ~90% of resistance); absence of viral TK. c) Foscarnet - nephrotoxic (AKI, ATN, dose related), divalent cation chelation (hypoCa 15-30%, hypoMg 15-45%, hypoK 10-15%, rare hyperCa/hypo-hyperPO). Cidofovir - nephrotoxic (dose related, accumulates in proximal renal tubular cells, Fanconi syndrome), neutropenia 25%.

questions.model_answer: a) Ganciclovir - viral DNA polymerase (UL54), acting at the dNTP/catalytic site as a competitive inhibitor of deoxyguanosine triphosphate incorporation (requires prior phosphorylation, initially by the UL97 kinase). Foscarnet - viral DNA polymerase (UL54), acting at the pyrophosphate-binding site. Maribavir - the viral UL97 protein kinase, blocking phosphorylation of substrates such as UL44 and thereby viral DNA synthesis and nuclear egress.

cohort_answer.text: Ganciclovir - inhibits viral DNA polymerase UL54 (via dNTP binding site/catalytic site). Foscarnet - inhibits viral DNA polymerase UL54 (via pyrophosphate binding site). Maribavir - inhibits viral UL97 kinase, preventing nuclear egress. UL97 mutations confer resistance to ganciclovir/valganciclovir; UL54 mutation confers multidrug resistance.

questions.question: Letermovir is a new agent used to treat cytomegalovirus.
questions.question_raw: Q29 (2018). Letermovir is a new agent used to treat CMV

parts.text: What is its target?
What is the mechanism of action?

parts_raw.text: a) What is its target?
b) What is the MOA?

questions.model_answer:
a) The CMV terminase enzyme complex, specifically the UL56 subunit (the complex comprises UL51, UL56, with UL89); UL56 mutation mediates letermovir resistance.
b) The terminase complex cleaves concatemeric viral DNA into unit-length genomes and packages them into capsids; letermovir binds and inhibits this terminase, blocking DNA cleavage/packaging and viral maturation. It does not require phosphorylation and does not inhibit the viral DNA polymerase, so it is active against CMV isolates resistant to ganciclovir, cidofovir and foscarnet; it is active only against CMV among human herpesviruses.

cohort_answer.text: Target: UL56 (component of CMV terminase enzyme complex). MOA: terminase complex catalyzes cleavage and packaging of viral DNA; letermovir inhibits CMV replication by blocking cleavage/packaging; active against most CMV isolates resistant to other antivirals; doesn't need phosphorylation like ganciclovir; doesn't inhibit viral DNA polymerase like ganciclovir/cidofovir/foscarnet; only active against CMV.

questions.model_answer:
a) Ganciclovir: phosphorylated first by the viral UL97 kinase then by cellular kinases to ganciclovir triphosphate, which competitively inhibits the viral DNA polymerase (UL54) with respect to dGTP and slows/stops viral DNA chain elongation (not an obligate chain terminator).
b) Letermovir: inhibits the viral terminase complex (UL56/UL51/UL89), blocking cleavage and packaging of viral DNA; no phosphorylation required and no DNA-polymerase inhibition.
c) Foscarnet: pyrophosphate analogue that directly inhibits the viral DNA polymerase (UL54) at the pyrophosphate-binding site; requires no phosphorylation.
d) Maribavir: inhibits the UL97 protein kinase, reducing phosphorylation of UL44 and other proteins, thereby inhibiting viral DNA synthesis and blocking nuclear egress of virions.
e) (1) UL97 gene mutation (phosphotransferase/protein kinase) - point mutations or deletions reduce intracellular ganciclovir phosphorylation, causing ganciclovir resistance while isolates remain susceptible to foscarnet and cidofovir. (2) UL54 gene mutation (viral DNA polymerase) - point mutations cause ganciclovir resistance and can confer cross-resistance to cidofovir and foscarnet.
questions.beyond_mandell: Foscarnet's pyrophosphate-binding-site detail is established knowledge; the text grounds foscarnet as a DNA-polymerase inhibitor (p.591) and the ganciclovir (p.589), letermovir (pp.591-592) and maribavir (p.592) mechanisms and the UL97/UL54 resistance mutations (p.589).

cohort_answer.text: Ganciclovir - binds UL54 catalytic site of DNA polymerase. Letermovir - binds UL89/56/51 DNA terminase complex, inhibits viral maturation. Foscarnet - binds UL54 DNA polymerase pyrophosphate site. Maribavir - pUL97 kinase inhibitor. Resistance mutations: point mutations in viral DNA polymerase (UL54 gene) - may cause resistance to ganciclovir/foscarnet/cidofovir (some knock out all three); reduced intracellular ganciclovir phosphorylation from point mutations/deletions in phosphotransferase encoded by UL97 gene (susceptible to foscarnet/cidofovir).

questions.model_answer: Key distinguishing reasons for each pair: Valganciclovir over valacyclovir - CMV activity. Famciclovir over acyclovir - better oral bioavailability/less frequent dosing for HSV/VZV. Atovaquone over dapsone - G6PD deficiency (avoid dapsone hemolysis). Doxycycline over TMP-SMX - G6PD deficiency or need to avoid sulfa/renal dosing. Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate - less nephrotoxicity/infusion toxicity. Fluconazole over caspofungin - need CNS/urinary penetration or oral therapy (azole penetrates; echinocandins do not). Azithromycin over clarithromycin - fewer CYP3A4 drug interactions. Metronidazole over clindamycin - avoid C. difficile risk. Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin - better anaerobic/respiratory coverage (conversely levofloxacin for urinary/renal penetration). Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem - carbapenem-sparing to reduce resistance pressure when adequate. Ampicillin over cloxacillin - Enterococcus or Listeria coverage. Cefazolin over cloxacillin - convenient dosing/efficacy for MSSA (or penicillin allergy considerations).
